title: Trigonometry
description: Trigonometry from the first angle through a full college course: degrees and radians, arc length and angular speed, right-triangle trig, the unit circle, graphs of all six functions and sinusoidal models, inverse functions, identities and equations, the laws of sines and cosines, vectors, polar coordinates, parametric equations, and complex numbers in trigonometric form with De Moivre's theorem.
author: Examiner
changelog: Checked against university and open-textbook sources; corrected missing conditions in rules and definitions, added a few short sections, and added a lesson on parametric equations.

lessons.title: Angles and degree measure
lessons.body:
## What trigonometry is about

Trigonometry began as the study of triangles: how the angles of a triangle control the
lengths of its sides. Surveyors, sailors and astronomers needed it to measure distances
they could not walk. Over time it grew into the study of anything that rotates or
repeats: a wheel, a pendulum, a sound wave, an alternating current. Every one of those
starts with the same object, the angle, so that is where this course starts.

In geometry an angle is a static figure made of two rays. In trigonometry we think of an
angle as a **[[rotation]]**. That small change of viewpoint is what lets angles be negative,
or bigger than a full turn, and it is what makes the rest of the subject work.

## Angles as rotations

An **[[angle]]** is formed by rotating a ray about its endpoint. The ray's starting position
is the **[[initial side]]**, its final position is the **[[terminal side]]**, and the common
endpoint is the **[[vertex]]**. The angle measures how far, and in which direction, the ray
turned.

- A counterclockwise rotation gives a **[[positive angle]]**.
- A clockwise rotation gives a **[[negative angle]]**.

An angle is in **[[standard position]]** when its vertex is at the origin of the coordinate
plane and its initial side lies along the positive $x$-axis. Then the terminal side alone
tells you where the angle "points", and we say the angle *lies in* the quadrant that
contains its terminal side.

```plot
{"x": [-3, 3], "y": [-3, 3], "equal": true, "segments": [{"from": [0, 0], "to": [2.6, 0], "arrow": true, "label": "initial side"}, {"from": [0, 0], "to": [-1.3, 2.25], "arrow": true, "label": "terminal side"}], "curves": [{"x": "0.8cos(t)", "y": "0.8sin(t)", "t": [0, 2.0944]}], "labels": [{"at": [0.75, 0.75], "text": "120°"}], "caption": "An angle of 120° in standard position; it lies in quadrant II"}
```

When the terminal side lies on an axis (0°, 90°, 180°, 270°, …) the angle is a
**[[quadrantal angle]]** and lies in no quadrant.

## Degree measure

The **[[degree]]** divides one full counterclockwise rotation into 360 equal parts, so a full
turn is $360^\circ$, a half turn is $180^\circ$ and a quarter turn is $90^\circ$. The number
360 is a legacy of Babylonian astronomy (it has many divisors, which made fractions of a
turn easy), not anything forced by geometry. The next lesson introduces a measure that
*is* forced by geometry.

Familiar names describe the size of an angle between $0^\circ$ and $180^\circ$:

| Name | Measure |
|---|---|
| **[[acute angle]]** | between $0^\circ$ and $90^\circ$ |
| **[[right angle]]** | exactly $90^\circ$ |
| **[[obtuse angle]]** | between $90^\circ$ and $180^\circ$ |
| **[[straight angle]]** | exactly $180^\circ$ |

Two positive angles are **[[complementary]]** if they add to $90^\circ$ and **[[supplementary]]**
if they add to $180^\circ$. The complement of $35^\circ$ is $55^\circ$; its supplement is
$145^\circ$. An angle of $110^\circ$ has a supplement ($70^\circ$) but no positive complement.

### Minutes and seconds

For finer measurement, a degree is split into 60 **[[minutes]]** and a minute into 60
**[[seconds]]**: $1^\circ = 60'$ and $1' = 60''$, so $1^\circ = 3600''$. This
**[[degrees–minutes–seconds (DMS)]]** notation is still used in navigation, surveying and
astronomy. Converting is just a change of units.

$$\theta = D^\circ\,M'\,S'' \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \theta = D + \frac{M}{60} + \frac{S}{3600}\ \text{degrees}$$

### Example 1

Convert $47^\circ 21' 36''$ to decimal degrees, and convert $18.715^\circ$ to DMS.

**Step 1 (DMS to decimal).** Each minute is $\tfrac1{60}$ of a degree and each second is
$\tfrac1{3600}$ of a degree:
$$47 + \frac{21}{60} + \frac{36}{3600} = 47 + 0.35 + 0.01 = 47.36^\circ.$$

**Step 2 (decimal to DMS).** Keep the whole part, $18^\circ$. Multiply the leftover
fraction by 60 to get minutes: $0.715 \times 60 = 42.9'$. Keep $42'$ and multiply the new
leftover by 60 to get seconds: $0.9 \times 60 = 54''$. So $18.715^\circ = 18^\circ 42' 54''$.

## Coterminal angles

Rotating an extra full turn, in either direction, brings the terminal side back to the
same place. Angles in standard position with the same terminal side are **coterminal
angles**. Because a full turn is $360^\circ$,

$$\theta \text{ and } \theta + 360^\circ k \text{ are coterminal for every integer } k.$$

Coterminal angles will turn out to have identical trigonometric values, so a standard
move in this course is to replace an angle by the coterminal angle in $[0^\circ, 360^\circ)$.
To find it, add or subtract $360^\circ$ until you land in that interval. For large
angles, divide by 360 to see how many full turns to remove.

```plot
{"x": [-3, 3], "y": [-3, 3], "equal": true, "segments": [{"from": [0, 0], "to": [2.6, 0], "arrow": true}, {"from": [0, 0], "to": [1.84, -1.84], "arrow": true}], "curves": [{"x": "0.7cos(t)", "y": "0.7sin(t)", "t": [0, 5.4978]}, {"x": "1.2cos(t)", "y": "1.2sin(t)", "t": [-0.7854, 0]}], "labels": [{"at": [-1.1, 0.9], "text": "315°"}, {"at": [1.7, -0.45], "text": "−45°"}], "caption": "315° and −45° share a terminal side, so they are coterminal"}
```

### Example 2

Find the angle in $[0^\circ, 360^\circ)$ coterminal with (a) $-250^\circ$ and (b) $1000^\circ$,
and name the quadrant of each.

**(a)** $-250^\circ$ is negative, so add one full turn: $-250^\circ + 360^\circ = 110^\circ$.
That is between $90^\circ$ and $180^\circ$, so the angle lies in **quadrant II**.

**(b)** $1000 \div 360 \approx 2.78$, so two full turns can be removed:
$1000^\circ - 2(360^\circ) = 280^\circ$. That is between $270^\circ$ and $360^\circ$: **quadrant IV**.

A quick check: $280 + 720 = 1000$. ✓

### Example 3

A Ferris wheel car starts at the far right of the wheel and the wheel turns clockwise
through $2\tfrac14$ revolutions. What angle in standard position describes the rotation,
and what positive angle less than $360^\circ$ is coterminal with it?

Clockwise means negative: $-2.25 \times 360^\circ = -810^\circ$. Add $360^\circ$ three
times: $-810^\circ + 1080^\circ = 270^\circ$. The car ends straight below the center,
which matches a quadrantal angle of $270^\circ$.

## Common mistakes

- **Mixing up the sign convention.** Counterclockwise is positive. A clockwise quarter
  turn is $-90^\circ$, which is coterminal with $270^\circ$, not $90^\circ$.
- **Treating minutes as decimals.** $25^\circ 30'$ is $25.5^\circ$, not $25.3^\circ$:
  30 minutes is half a degree.
- **Stopping too early with coterminal angles.** $-400^\circ + 360^\circ = -40^\circ$
  is still negative; add another $360^\circ$ to get $320^\circ$.
- **Confusing complement and supplement.** "C" comes before "S", and 90 comes before 180.

## Key points

- An angle is a rotation from an initial side to a terminal side; counterclockwise is
  positive.
- Standard position: vertex at the origin, initial side on the positive $x$-axis.
- $360^\circ$ is one full turn; $1^\circ = 60'$ and $1' = 60''$.
- Coterminal angles differ by a whole number of full turns: $\theta + 360^\circ k$.
- To find the coterminal angle in $[0^\circ, 360^\circ)$, add or subtract $360^\circ$
  until you land in the interval.

lessons.title: Radian measure
lessons.body:
## Why a second unit?

Degrees are convenient for everyday angles, but the number 360 is arbitrary. Calculus,
physics and the formulas later in this course all become simpler when angles are
measured in a unit that comes from the circle itself. That unit is the radian. After this
lesson you should be able to move between degrees and radians without hesitation, and
you should start to *think* in radians for the common angles.

## What a radian is

Draw a circle of radius $r$ and put the vertex of an angle at its center. An angle whose
vertex is at the center of a circle is a **[[central angle]]**, and the piece of the circle
between its sides is the arc it *subtends*. One **[[radian]]** is the central angle that
subtends an arc exactly as long as the radius.

```plot
{"x": [-1.6, 1.6], "y": [-1.4, 1.6], "equal": true, "circles": [{"center": [0, 0], "r": 1}], "segments": [{"from": [0, 0], "to": [1, 0], "label": "r"}, {"from": [0, 0], "to": [0.5403, 0.8415], "label": "r"}], "curves": [{"x": "1.0cos(t)", "y": "1.0sin(t)", "t": [0, 1], "color": "#d9480f"}, {"x": "0.3cos(t)", "y": "0.3sin(t)", "t": [0, 1]}], "labels": [{"at": [1.2, 0.6], "text": "arc = r"}, {"at": [0.45, 0.2], "text": "1 rad"}], "caption": "One radian: the arc is as long as the radius"}
```

Because the definition compares two lengths, the radian measure of an angle is
$$\theta = \frac{\text{arc length}}{\text{radius}} = \frac{s}{r},$$
a pure number with no units. That is why "radians" is often left off: if an angle is
written with no degree sign, it is in radians. $\sin 2$ means the sine of 2 radians, not
2 degrees.

The radian measure of an angle doesn't depend on the size of the circle: doubling the
radius doubles the arc as well, and the ratio stays the same.

## The conversion factor

A full turn subtends the whole circumference, $2\pi r$. Dividing by $r$:

$$\text{one full turn} = 2\pi \text{ radians} = 360^\circ, \qquad \pi \text{ radians} = 180^\circ.$$

Everything else follows from $\pi = 180^\circ$. Multiply by a form of 1:

$$\text{degrees} \to \text{radians: multiply by } \frac{\pi}{180^\circ}, \qquad \text{radians} \to \text{degrees: multiply by } \frac{180^\circ}{\pi}.$$

One radian is $\tfrac{180^\circ}{\pi} \approx 57.296^\circ$, a bit less than $60^\circ$.
That's a useful sanity check: $2$ radians is about $115^\circ$, $3$ radians is a bit less
than a half turn, and $6.28$ radians is about one full turn.

### Example 1

Convert $135^\circ$ and $-210^\circ$ to radians. Give exact answers.

$$135^\circ \cdot \frac{\pi}{180^\circ} = \frac{135\pi}{180} = \frac{3\pi}{4}.$$
To simplify $\tfrac{135}{180}$, divide top and bottom by 45.

$$-210^\circ \cdot \frac{\pi}{180^\circ} = -\frac{210\pi}{180} = -\frac{7\pi}{6}.$$

Exact answers keep $\pi$ as a symbol. $\tfrac{3\pi}{4} \approx 2.356$ is a decimal
approximation, useful for a calculator but not the exact value.

### Example 2

Convert $\dfrac{5\pi}{3}$ and $2.5$ radians to degrees.

$$\frac{5\pi}{3}\cdot\frac{180^\circ}{\pi} = \frac{5 \cdot 180^\circ}{3} = 300^\circ.$$
The $\pi$ cancels, which is what you expect when the radian measure is a multiple of $\pi$.

$$2.5 \cdot \frac{180^\circ}{\pi} = \frac{450^\circ}{\pi} \approx 143.24^\circ.$$
Here no $\pi$ cancels, so the answer is a decimal.

## Thinking in radians

The angles you'll meet constantly are fractions of $\pi$. It pays to learn them as
fractions of a half turn rather than converting every time:

| Degrees | 0° | 30° | 45° | 60° | 90° | 120° | 135° | 150° | 180° | 270° | 360° |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Radians | $0$ | $\frac{\pi}{6}$ | $\frac{\pi}{4}$ | $\frac{\pi}{3}$ | $\frac{\pi}{2}$ | $\frac{2\pi}{3}$ | $\frac{3\pi}{4}$ | $\frac{5\pi}{6}$ | $\pi$ | $\frac{3\pi}{2}$ | $2\pi$ |

A good habit: read $\tfrac{5\pi}{6}$ as "five sixths of a half turn", which is
$5 \times 30^\circ = 150^\circ$. The denominator tells you the step size
($\pi/6 = 30^\circ$, $\pi/4 = 45^\circ$, $\pi/3 = 60^\circ$) and the numerator counts steps.

### Coterminal angles in radians

A full turn is $2\pi$, so $\theta$ and $\theta + 2\pi k$ are coterminal. To find the
coterminal angle in $[0, 2\pi)$, add or subtract multiples of $2\pi$.

### Example 3

Find the angle in $[0, 2\pi)$ coterminal with $\dfrac{17\pi}{4}$, and with $-\dfrac{5\pi}{6}$.

$2\pi = \tfrac{8\pi}{4}$, so subtract it twice: $\tfrac{17\pi}{4} - \tfrac{16\pi}{4} = \tfrac{\pi}{4}$.

For the negative angle, add $2\pi = \tfrac{12\pi}{6}$: $-\tfrac{5\pi}{6} + \tfrac{12\pi}{6} = \tfrac{7\pi}{6}$,
which is in quadrant III (between $\pi$ and $\tfrac{3\pi}{2}$).

```plot
{"x": [-1.5, 1.5], "y": [-1.5, 1.5], "equal": true, "circles": [{"center": [0, 0], "r": 1}], "segments": [{"from": [0, 0], "to": [1.2, 0]}, {"from": [0, 0], "to": [-0.866, -0.5], "arrow": true}], "curves": [{"x": "0.5cos(t)", "y": "0.5sin(t)", "t": [-2.618, 0]}], "labels": [{"at": [0.25, -0.65], "text": "−5π/6"}, {"at": [-1.15, -0.65], "text": "7π/6"}], "caption": "−5π/6 and 7π/6 end on the same ray in quadrant III"}
```

## Quadrants in radians

| Quadrant | Degrees | Radians |
|---|---|---|
| I | $0^\circ < \theta < 90^\circ$ | $0 < \theta < \frac{\pi}{2}$ |
| II | $90^\circ < \theta < 180^\circ$ | $\frac{\pi}{2} < \theta < \pi$ |
| III | $180^\circ < \theta < 270^\circ$ | $\pi < \theta < \frac{3\pi}{2}$ |
| IV | $270^\circ < \theta < 360^\circ$ | $\frac{3\pi}{2} < \theta < 2\pi$ |

For an angle like $4$ radians, compare with $\pi \approx 3.14$ and
$\tfrac{3\pi}{2} \approx 4.71$: since $3.14 < 4 < 4.71$, the angle lies in quadrant III.

## A note on calculators and software

Spreadsheets and programming languages always work in radians, and a calculator works in
whichever mode it is set to (many default to radians). In a spreadsheet, `SIN(30)` is the sine of 30 radians; you would write
`SIN(RADIANS(30))` for $30^\circ$. Graphing tools label the $x$-axis in radians for the same
reason. Getting comfortable with radians now saves a lot of confusion later, when trig
functions are graphed and when calculus formulas such as "the derivative of $\sin x$ is
$\cos x$" turn out to be true only in radians.

## Common mistakes

- **Using the wrong conversion factor.** Going to radians, $\pi$ goes on top. A check:
  degrees are "big numbers", radians are "small numbers", so $90^\circ$ should become
  something near 1.6, not near 5000.
- **Forgetting that a bare number is radians.** $\sin 30$ on a calculator in radian mode
  is $\sin(30 \text{ rad})$, about $-0.988$, not $\tfrac12$. Check the mode.
- **Not reducing fractions.** $\tfrac{150\pi}{180}$ should be written $\tfrac{5\pi}{6}$.
- **Thinking $\pi$ means $180$ as a number.** $\pi$ radians is an angle *equal to*
  $180^\circ$; the number $\pi$ itself is still $3.14159\ldots$

## Key points

- One radian subtends an arc equal to the radius; $\theta = s/r$ has no units.
- $\pi \text{ rad} = 180^\circ$ and $2\pi \text{ rad} = 360^\circ$.
- Degrees to radians: multiply by $\pi/180$. Radians to degrees: multiply by $180/\pi$.
- $1 \text{ rad} \approx 57.3^\circ$.
- An angle written with no units is in radians; coterminal angles differ by $2\pi k$.

lessons.title: Arc length and sector area
lessons.body:
## From the definition of a radian to two formulas

The last lesson defined radian measure as a ratio: $\theta = s/r$. Read backward, that
definition is a formula for the length of an arc, and a short proportion turns it into a
formula for the area of a pie-shaped slice. Both formulas are *only* this simple in
radians, which is the first concrete payoff for learning the new unit.

## Arc length

An **[[arc]]** is the part of a circle between two points on it. If a central angle of
$\theta$ radians subtends an arc on a circle of radius $r$, the **[[arc length]]** is

$$s = r\theta \qquad (\theta \text{ in radians}).$$

**Why:** by definition $\theta = s/r$; multiply both sides by $r$. Another way to see it:
the full circumference $2\pi r$ belongs to the full angle $2\pi$, so each radian of angle
"buys" $r$ units of arc.

If the angle is given in degrees, convert it first. Equivalently, the arc is the fraction
$\tfrac{\theta^\circ}{360^\circ}$ of the whole circumference:
$s = \tfrac{\theta^\circ}{360^\circ}\cdot 2\pi r$, which is the same formula in disguise.

```plot
{"x": [-1.3, 1.5], "y": [-0.4, 1.4], "equal": true, "segments": [{"from": [0, 0], "to": [1.2, 0], "label": "r"}, {"from": [0, 0], "to": [-0.3106, 1.1591], "label": "r"}], "curves": [{"x": "1.2cos(t)", "y": "1.2sin(t)", "t": [0, 1.8326], "color": "#d9480f"}, {"x": "0.3cos(t)", "y": "0.3sin(t)", "t": [0, 1.8326]}], "labels": [{"at": [1.15, 0.85], "text": "s = rθ"}, {"at": [0.35, 0.35], "text": "θ"}], "caption": "The arc subtended by a central angle θ"}
```

### Example 1

A circle has radius 8 cm. Find the length of the arc subtended by a central angle of
$135^\circ$.

**Step 1: convert to radians.** $135^\circ \cdot \tfrac{\pi}{180^\circ} = \tfrac{3\pi}{4}$.

**Step 2: apply $s = r\theta$.** $s = 8 \cdot \tfrac{3\pi}{4} = 6\pi \approx 18.85$ cm.

**Check:** $135^\circ$ is $\tfrac{3}{8}$ of a full turn, and the full circumference is
$16\pi$; $\tfrac38 \cdot 16\pi = 6\pi$. ✓

### Example 2

Two towns lie on the same north–south line (meridian), at latitudes $40^\circ 15'$ N and
$32^\circ 45'$ N. Treating Earth as a sphere of radius 3960 miles, how far apart are they
along the surface?

The central angle between them is the difference in latitude:
$40^\circ 15' - 32^\circ 45' = 7^\circ 30' = 7.5^\circ$.

In radians: $7.5 \cdot \tfrac{\pi}{180} = \tfrac{\pi}{24}$.

$s = r\theta = 3960 \cdot \tfrac{\pi}{24} = 165\pi \approx 518.4$ miles.

## Finding the angle or the radius

The same formula solves for any one of the three quantities:
$$\theta = \frac{s}{r}, \qquad r = \frac{s}{\theta}.$$
If an arc of 15 m sits on a circle of radius 6 m, the angle is $\theta = 15/6 = 2.5$ radians,
which is about $143.2^\circ$.

## Sector area

A **[[sector]]** is the pie-slice region bounded by two radii and the arc between them. Its
area is a fraction of the whole disk's area $\pi r^2$, and that fraction is
$\tfrac{\theta}{2\pi}$:

$$A = \frac{\theta}{2\pi}\cdot \pi r^2 = \frac12 r^2\theta \qquad (\theta \text{ in radians}).$$

In degrees the same idea reads $A = \tfrac{\theta^\circ}{360^\circ}\,\pi r^2$.

Notice that $A = \tfrac12 r^2\theta = \tfrac12 r \cdot (r\theta) = \tfrac12 r s$. A thin sector
looks like a triangle with base $s$ and height $r$, and the formula matches
$\tfrac12 \cdot \text{base} \cdot \text{height}$.

### Example 3

A lawn sprinkler sprays water 18 ft and sweeps back and forth through $110^\circ$. What
area does it water?

**Step 1:** $110^\circ = \tfrac{110\pi}{180} = \tfrac{11\pi}{18}$ radians.

**Step 2:** $A = \tfrac12 (18)^2 \cdot \tfrac{11\pi}{18} = \tfrac12 \cdot 324 \cdot \tfrac{11\pi}{18} = 99\pi \approx 311.0 \text{ ft}^2.$

**Check with degrees:** $\tfrac{110}{360}\cdot \pi \cdot 324 = 99\pi$. ✓

```plot
{"x": [-1.4, 1.4], "y": [-0.5, 1.4], "equal": true, "polygons": [{"points": [[0, 0], [1.2, 0], [1.1276, 0.4104], [0.9192, 0.7713], [0.6, 1.0392], [0.2084, 1.1818], [-0.2084, 1.1818], [-0.4104, 1.1276], [0, 0]], "fill": true}], "labels": [{"at": [0.3, 0.45], "text": "sector"}], "caption": "A sector: the region between two radii and their arc (here about 110°)"}
```

## Units

- In $s = r\theta$, $s$ has the units of $r$ (radians carry no units).
- In $A = \tfrac12 r^2\theta$, $A$ has the units of $r^2$.
- The angle must be in radians. Plugging in degrees is the single most common error with
  these formulas, and it gives answers about 57 times too big.

### Example 4: an area between two arcs

A car's windshield wiper is 22 in long from the pivot to its tip, but the rubber blade only
covers the part from 6 in to 22 in out. The arm sweeps through $120^\circ$. What area does the blade
clean?

The cleaned region is a big sector (radius 22) minus a small sector (radius 6), both with
$\theta = \tfrac{2\pi}{3}$:
$$A = \tfrac12(22)^2\cdot\tfrac{2\pi}{3} - \tfrac12(6)^2\cdot\tfrac{2\pi}{3} = \tfrac{\pi}{3}(484 - 36) = \tfrac{448\pi}{3} \approx 469.1 \text{ in}^2.$$
Factoring out $\tfrac12\theta$ first, $A = \tfrac12\theta(R^2 - r^2)$, saves a step whenever two sectors share
an angle.

## Arc length versus chord length

The arc is the curved path along the circle; the **[[chord]]** is the straight segment joining its
endpoints. The chord is always shorter. For a $60^\circ$ angle on a circle of radius 10, the arc is
$10\cdot\tfrac{\pi}{3} \approx 10.47$, while the chord (a side of an equilateral triangle) is exactly 10. For
small angles the two are nearly equal, which is why a short stretch of a huge circle, like a
mile of Earth's surface, looks straight.

## Common mistakes

- **Degrees in a radian formula.** $s = 8 \cdot 135$ is not an arc length. Convert first.
- **Using diameter for radius.** A 20-inch wheel usually means the diameter; $r = 10$ in.
- **Mixing up $s = r\theta$ and $A = \tfrac12 r^2\theta$.** Area involves $r^2$ and the
  factor $\tfrac12$; length involves $r$ alone.
- **Forgetting latitude differences in DMS.** $7^\circ 30'$ is $7.5^\circ$, not $7.3^\circ$.

## Key points

- Arc length: $s = r\theta$ with $\theta$ in radians.
- Sector area: $A = \tfrac12 r^2\theta = \tfrac12 rs$ with $\theta$ in radians.
- In degrees, use the fraction of a full turn: $\tfrac{\theta}{360}$ of the circumference
  or of the area.
- Solve the same formulas for $\theta$ or $r$ when those are unknown.

lessons.title: Angular and linear speed
lessons.body:
## Two ways to say "how fast"

A point on a spinning wheel moves in two senses at once. Its radius line sweeps out angle,
and the point itself travels along the circle. The first is described by *angular* speed
(how much angle per unit time) and the second by *linear* speed (how much distance per
unit time). The arc length formula from the last lesson connects them, so this lesson is
really $s = r\theta$ divided by time.

## Definitions

Suppose a point moves along a circle of radius $r$ at a steady rate, sweeping out an
angle $\theta$ (in radians) and traveling an arc length $s$ in time $t$.

- The **[[angular speed]]** is the angle swept per unit time: $\omega = \dfrac{\theta}{t}$.
  Typical units are radians per second (rad/s) or radians per minute.
- The **[[linear speed]]** is the distance traveled per unit time: $v = \dfrac{s}{t}$.
  Typical units are m/s, ft/s, mi/h.

The Greek letter $\omega$ (omega) is the standard symbol for angular speed.

## The connecting formula

Divide $s = r\theta$ by $t$:

$$\frac{s}{t} = r\cdot\frac{\theta}{t} \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad v = r\omega \quad (\omega \text{ in radians per unit time}).$$

Every point on a rigid spinning disk has the *same* angular speed, but points farther from
the center travel bigger circles in the same time, so their linear speed is bigger in
proportion to $r$. On a merry-go-round, the outer horses move faster than the inner ones.

```plot
{"x": [-1.6, 1.6], "y": [-1.4, 1.4], "equal": true, "circles": [{"center": [0, 0], "r": 1.2}, {"center": [0, 0], "r": 0.6}], "segments": [{"from": [0.6, 0], "to": [0.6, 0.35], "arrow": true}, {"from": [1.2, 0], "to": [1.2, 0.7], "arrow": true}, {"from": [0, 0], "to": [1.2, 0], "dashed": true}], "points": [[0.6, 0], [1.2, 0]], "labels": [{"at": [0.85, 0.5], "text": "v"}, {"at": [1.45, 0.85], "text": "2v"}], "caption": "Same angular speed; doubling the radius doubles the linear speed"}
```

## Revolutions per minute

Motors, wheels and disks are usually rated in **[[revolutions per minute (rpm)]]**. Since one
revolution is $2\pi$ radians,

$$\omega \ (\text{rad/min}) = 2\pi \times (\text{rpm}).$$

To get rad/s, also divide by 60. Going the other way, rpm $= \omega / (2\pi)$ when $\omega$
is in rad/min. Note that rpm is an angular speed in disguise: it counts turns per minute,
not distance.

### Example 1

A car's tires have radius 14 inches and are turning at 300 rpm. Find the tires'
angular speed in rad/min and the car's speed in miles per hour.

**Step 1: angular speed.** $\omega = 300 \cdot 2\pi = 600\pi$ rad/min.

**Step 2: linear speed.** A point on the tread moves at $v = r\omega = 14 \cdot 600\pi = 8400\pi$
inches per minute, about $26{,}389$ in/min. When a tire rolls without slipping, the car
moves at the same speed as the tread relative to the axle.

**Step 3: convert units.** There are 60 minutes in an hour and $5280 \times 12 = 63{,}360$
inches in a mile:
$$8400\pi \,\frac{\text{in}}{\text{min}} \cdot \frac{60 \text{ min}}{1 \text{ h}} \cdot \frac{1 \text{ mi}}{63{,}360 \text{ in}} \approx 25.0 \text{ mi/h}.$$

Unit conversion is where most errors in these problems happen. Writing each factor as a
fraction whose units cancel keeps it honest.

### Example 2

Earth turns once on its axis about every 24 hours. Its equatorial radius is about 3960
miles. How fast is a point on the equator moving because of the rotation?

$\omega = \dfrac{2\pi \text{ rad}}{24 \text{ h}} = \dfrac{\pi}{12}$ rad/h.

$v = r\omega = 3960 \cdot \dfrac{\pi}{12} = 330\pi \approx 1037$ mi/h.

People on the equator are moving over a thousand miles per hour and don't feel it,
because the speed is steady.

### Example 3: belts and gears

A belt connects a pulley of radius 5 cm to a pulley of radius 15 cm. The small pulley
spins at 12 rad/s. How fast does the large pulley spin?

The belt doesn't slip, so every point on the belt, and the rim of each pulley, has the same
linear speed:
$$v = r_1\omega_1 = 5 \cdot 12 = 60 \text{ cm/s}.$$
For the large pulley, $\omega_2 = \dfrac{v}{r_2} = \dfrac{60}{15} = 4$ rad/s, about
$4 \cdot \tfrac{60}{2\pi} \approx 38.2$ rpm.

The bigger pulley turns slower, in inverse proportion to its radius:
$\omega_1 r_1 = \omega_2 r_2$. Bicycle gears work the same way, with the chain as the belt.

## Choosing the formula

| You know | You want | Use |
|---|---|---|
| angle and time | angular speed | $\omega = \theta/t$ |
| arc length and time | linear speed | $v = s/t$ |
| radius and angular speed | linear speed | $v = r\omega$ |
| radius and linear speed | angular speed | $\omega = v/r$ |
| rpm | rad/min | multiply by $2\pi$ |

### Example 4: bicycle gears

A cyclist pedals at 60 rpm. The front chainring has radius 10 cm and the rear sprocket has
radius 4 cm. The rear wheel (attached to the sprocket) has radius 35 cm. How fast is the
bicycle moving, in km/h?

**Chain speed.** The chain is a belt: the chainring and sprocket rims share its linear speed,
so $\omega_{\text{front}}r_{\text{front}} = \omega_{\text{rear}}r_{\text{rear}}$. In rpm,
$60 \cdot 10 = \omega_{\text{rear}}\cdot 4$, so the sprocket, and the wheel with it, turns at $150$ rpm.
(Ratios of rpm work just like ratios of rad/min, since the $2\pi$ cancels.)

**Wheel speed.** $v = r\omega = 35 \cdot 150 \cdot 2\pi \approx 32{,}987$ cm/min. Converting:
$32{,}987 \text{ cm/min} \times 60 \text{ min/h} \div 100{,}000 \text{ cm/km} \approx 19.8$ km/h.

## Common mistakes

- **Using rpm directly in $v = r\omega$.** $\omega$ must be in radians per unit time.
  $14 \times 300 = 4200$ is not a speed in any useful unit; multiply by $2\pi$ first.
- **Diameter versus radius.** A "26-inch bike wheel" has a 13-inch radius.
- **Mismatched time units.** If $\omega$ is per minute, $v$ is per minute. Convert at the
  end, and do it explicitly.
- **Thinking all points on a disk have the same linear speed.** They share $\omega$, not $v$.

## Key points

- Angular speed $\omega = \theta/t$ (radians per unit time); linear speed $v = s/t$.
- $v = r\omega$, valid only with $\omega$ in radians per unit time.
- One revolution is $2\pi$ radians, so rad/min $= 2\pi \times$ rpm.
- Linked pulleys or gears share linear speed: $r_1\omega_1 = r_2\omega_2$.

lessons.title: The six trigonometric ratios
lessons.body:
## Shape decides the ratios

Module 1 was about measuring angles. This module connects angles to lengths, and right
triangles are where that connection is simplest. The key fact comes from geometry: two
right triangles with the same acute angle are **[[similar]]**, so their sides are in the same
proportions no matter how big the triangles are. A ratio of two sides depends only on the
angle. Those ratios are the trigonometric functions.

```plot
{"x": [-0.5, 9], "y": [-0.5, 6.5], "equal": true, "polygons": [{"points": [[0, 0], [4, 0], [4, 3]]}, {"points": [[0, 0], [8, 0], [8, 6]], "color": "#1c7ed6", "fill": true}], "labels": [{"at": [1.3, 0.3], "text": "θ"}, {"at": [4.35, 1.5], "text": "3"}, {"at": [2.0, -0.35], "text": "4"}, {"at": [8.35, 3.0], "text": "6"}, {"at": [6.0, -0.35], "text": "8"}], "caption": "Same angle θ, different sizes: opposite/adjacent is 3/4 = 6/8 in both"}
```

## Naming the sides

Fix one acute angle $\theta$ of a right triangle. Relative to $\theta$:

- the **[[hypotenuse]]** is the side across from the right angle (always the longest side);
- the **[[opposite side]]** is the leg across from $\theta$;
- the **[[adjacent side]]** is the leg that touches $\theta$ and is not the hypotenuse.

"Opposite" and "adjacent" depend on which acute angle you are looking at. Switch to the
other acute angle and the two legs trade names; the hypotenuse never changes.

```shape
{"polygons": [{"points": [[0, 0], [6, 0], [6, 3.5]]}], "rightAngles": [[[6, 0], [0, 0], [6, 3.5]]], "labels": [{"at": [1.2, 0.3], "text": "θ"}, {"at": [3, -0.45], "text": "adjacent"}, {"at": [7.2, 1.75], "text": "opposite"}, {"at": [2.6, 2.3], "text": "hypotenuse"}]}
```

## The six ratios

$$\sin\theta = \frac{\text{opp}}{\text{hyp}}, \qquad \cos\theta = \frac{\text{adj}}{\text{hyp}}, \qquad \tan\theta = \frac{\text{opp}}{\text{adj}},$$
$$\csc\theta = \frac{\text{hyp}}{\text{opp}}, \qquad \sec\theta = \frac{\text{hyp}}{\text{adj}}, \qquad \cot\theta = \frac{\text{adj}}{\text{opp}}.$$

The names are **[[sine]]**, **[[cosine]]**, **[[tangent]]**, **[[cosecant]]**, **[[secant]]** and
**[[cotangent]]**. The mnemonic **[[SOH-CAH-TOA]]** covers the first three: Sine = Opposite over
Hypotenuse, Cosine = Adjacent over Hypotenuse, Tangent = Opposite over Adjacent.

The second row is the first row flipped. These **[[reciprocal]]** relationships are worth
memorizing in this form:
$$\csc\theta = \frac{1}{\sin\theta}, \qquad \sec\theta = \frac{1}{\cos\theta}, \qquad \cot\theta = \frac{1}{\tan\theta}.$$
A common slip is pairing secant with sine. Each "co-" function in the bottom row is paired
with a function *without* "co" in the top row, and vice versa: **[[sec]]** pairs with **[[cos]]**,
**[[csc]]** with **[[sin]]**.

Since $\tan\theta = \tfrac{\text{opp}}{\text{adj}}$, dividing the top and bottom by the
hypotenuse shows $\tan\theta = \dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}$, and similarly
$\cot\theta = \dfrac{\cos\theta}{\sin\theta}$.

Because the hypotenuse is the longest side, $\sin\theta$ and $\cos\theta$ are always
between 0 and 1 for an acute angle, while $\csc\theta$ and $\sec\theta$ are always greater
than 1. Tangent and cotangent can be any positive number.

## Finding a missing side first

Often only two sides are known. The **[[Pythagorean theorem]]**, $a^2 + b^2 = c^2$ with $c$ the
hypotenuse, supplies the third. Whole-number solutions like $3, 4, 5$ and $5, 12, 13$ are
called **[[Pythagorean triples]]**; they make exact answers tidy, which is why textbook
problems love them.

### Example 1

A right triangle has legs 5 and 12. Let $\theta$ be the angle opposite the side of
length 5. Find all six trig ratios of $\theta$.

**Step 1: the hypotenuse.** $c = \sqrt{5^2 + 12^2} = \sqrt{169} = 13$.

**Step 2: label relative to $\theta$.** Opposite $= 5$, adjacent $= 12$, hypotenuse $= 13$.

**Step 3: write the ratios.**
$$\sin\theta = \tfrac{5}{13},\quad \cos\theta = \tfrac{12}{13},\quad \tan\theta = \tfrac{5}{12},\quad \csc\theta = \tfrac{13}{5},\quad \sec\theta = \tfrac{13}{12},\quad \cot\theta = \tfrac{12}{5}.$$

Check: the bottom three are the reciprocals of the top three, and $\sin$ and $\cos$ are
both below 1.

### Example 2

$\theta$ is acute and $\sin\theta = \tfrac37$. Find the other five ratios.

**Step 1: draw a triangle that fits.** Any right triangle with opposite 3 and hypotenuse 7
works, because only the ratio matters.

**Step 2: find the adjacent side.** $\text{adj} = \sqrt{7^2 - 3^2} = \sqrt{40} = 2\sqrt{10}$.

**Step 3: write the ratios and rationalize.**
$$\cos\theta = \frac{2\sqrt{10}}{7}, \quad \tan\theta = \frac{3}{2\sqrt{10}} = \frac{3\sqrt{10}}{20}, \quad \csc\theta = \frac73,$$
$$\sec\theta = \frac{7}{2\sqrt{10}} = \frac{7\sqrt{10}}{20}, \quad \cot\theta = \frac{2\sqrt{10}}{3}.$$
To rationalize $\tfrac{3}{2\sqrt{10}}$, multiply top and bottom by $\sqrt{10}$:
$\tfrac{3\sqrt{10}}{2 \cdot 10}$.

```shape
{"polygons": [{"points": [[0, 0], [6.3246, 0], [6.3246, 3]]}], "rightAngles": [[[6.3246, 0], [0, 0], [6.3246, 3]]], "labels": [{"at": [1.4, 0.3], "text": "θ"}, {"at": [3.16, -0.45], "text": "2√10"}, {"at": [6.75, 1.5], "text": "3"}, {"at": [2.9, 2.0], "text": "7"}], "caption": "A triangle with sin θ = 3/7"}
```

## Using a calculator

Calculators have keys for $\sin$, $\cos$ and $\tan$ only. For the others, use the
reciprocals: $\sec 40^\circ = \dfrac{1}{\cos 40^\circ} \approx \dfrac{1}{0.7660} \approx 1.3054$.
Make sure the calculator is in degree mode when the angle is in degrees.

Do **not** use the $\cos^{-1}$ key to find secant. $\cos^{-1}$ is the inverse cosine (it
takes a ratio and returns an angle), which is a completely different thing from
$\tfrac{1}{\cos}$. That distinction gets its own lesson in Module 5.

### Example 3

Find $\cot 25^\circ$ to four decimal places.

$\cot 25^\circ = \dfrac{1}{\tan 25^\circ} \approx \dfrac{1}{0.46631} \approx 2.1445$.

Sanity check: $25^\circ$ is a fairly small angle, so the opposite side is short compared
with the adjacent side, and adjacent/opposite should be bigger than 1. ✓

### Example 4: switching to the other acute angle

In Example 1's triangle (legs 5 and 12, hypotenuse 13), let $\beta$ be the *other* acute angle,
the one opposite the side of length 12. Find $\sin\beta$, $\cos\beta$ and $\tan\beta$.

From $\beta$, the opposite side is 12 and the adjacent side is 5:
$\sin\beta = \tfrac{12}{13}$, $\cos\beta = \tfrac{5}{13}$, $\tan\beta = \tfrac{12}{5}$.

Compare with $\theta$: $\sin\beta = \cos\theta$, $\cos\beta = \sin\theta$ and $\tan\beta = \cot\theta$. Because $\theta + \beta = 90^\circ$,
this always happens. The next lesson names it: the cofunction identities.

## Common mistakes

- **Labeling relative to the wrong angle.** Before writing any ratio, mark $\theta$ and
  label opposite/adjacent from *its* point of view.
- **Using the hypotenuse as a leg** in the Pythagorean theorem. The hypotenuse is alone
  on its side: $c^2 = a^2 + b^2$, so a leg is $\sqrt{c^2 - a^2}$.
- **Pairing secant with sine.** $\sec = 1/\cos$ and $\csc = 1/\sin$.
- **Confusing $\cos^{-1}$ with $\sec$.** $\cos^{-1}(0.5) = 60^\circ$ is an angle;
  $\sec 60^\circ = 2$ is a ratio.

## Key points

- Similar right triangles make each side ratio depend only on the angle.
- SOH-CAH-TOA: $\sin = \tfrac{\text{opp}}{\text{hyp}}$, $\cos = \tfrac{\text{adj}}{\text{hyp}}$,
  $\tan = \tfrac{\text{opp}}{\text{adj}}$.
- $\csc$, $\sec$, $\cot$ are the reciprocals of $\sin$, $\cos$, $\tan$.
- $\tan\theta = \sin\theta/\cos\theta$.
- Given one ratio, sketch a triangle, find the third side with the Pythagorean
  theorem, and read off the rest.

lessons.title: Special right triangles and cofunctions
lessons.body:
## Why some angles are special

For most angles, $\sin\theta$ is an endless decimal that you need a calculator for. For
three angles, $30^\circ$, $45^\circ$ and $60^\circ$, the trig ratios can be found exactly
with nothing but the Pythagorean theorem. These **[[exact values]]** come up constantly: in
graphs, in identities, in physics problems, and on every test that bans calculators. This
lesson derives them so you can rebuild them any time instead of memorizing a table.

## The 45°–45°–90° triangle

Cut a square of side 1 along its diagonal. Each half is a right triangle with two equal
legs of length 1 and two $45^\circ$ angles. By the Pythagorean theorem, the hypotenuse is
$\sqrt{1^2 + 1^2} = \sqrt{2}$.

```shape
{"polygons": [{"points": [[0, 0], [4, 0], [4, 4]]}], "rightAngles": [[[4, 0], [0, 0], [4, 4]]], "labels": [{"at": [1.0, 0.35], "text": "45°"}, {"at": [3.6, 2.9], "text": "45°"}, {"at": [2, -0.45], "text": "1"}, {"at": [4.4, 2], "text": "1"}, {"at": [1.6, 2.4], "text": "√2"}], "caption": "The 45°–45°–90° triangle: sides 1 : 1 : √2"}
```

So in every **[[45°–45°–90° triangle]]** the sides are in the ratio $1 : 1 : \sqrt2$:
the hypotenuse is $\sqrt2$ times a leg. Reading off the ratios,
$$\sin 45^\circ = \cos 45^\circ = \frac{1}{\sqrt2} = \frac{\sqrt2}{2}, \qquad \tan 45^\circ = 1.$$
Writing $\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}$ as $\tfrac{\sqrt2}{2}$ is called rationalizing the denominator.
Both forms are correct; $\tfrac{\sqrt2}{2}$ is the conventional one.

## The 30°–60°–90° triangle

Start with an equilateral triangle of side 2: all angles are $60^\circ$. Drop an altitude
from the top vertex. It bisects the base (into two pieces of length 1) and the top angle
(into two $30^\circ$ angles). Each half is a right triangle with hypotenuse 2, short leg 1,
and long leg $\sqrt{2^2 - 1^2} = \sqrt3$.

```shape
{"polygons": [{"points": [[0, 0], [4, 0], [2, 3.4641]]}], "segments": [{"from": [2, 0], "to": [2, 3.4641], "dashed": true}], "rightAngles": [[[2, 0], [4, 0], [2, 3.4641]]], "labels": [{"at": [0.7, 0.3], "text": "60°"}, {"at": [1.75, 2.6], "text": "30°"}, {"at": [1, -0.4], "text": "1"}, {"at": [3, -0.4], "text": "1"}, {"at": [0.6, 1.9], "text": "2"}, {"at": [2.4, 1.5], "text": "√3"}], "caption": "Half an equilateral triangle of side 2 is a 30°–60°–90° triangle"}
```

In every **[[30°–60°–90° triangle]]** the sides are in the ratio $1 : \sqrt3 : 2$
(short leg : long leg : hypotenuse). The short leg is opposite the $30^\circ$ angle and is
half the hypotenuse; the long leg is opposite $60^\circ$ and is $\sqrt3$ times the short leg.

From the $30^\circ$ angle: opposite $= 1$, adjacent $= \sqrt3$, hypotenuse $= 2$.
From the $60^\circ$ angle the legs swap roles.

| $\theta$ | $\sin\theta$ | $\cos\theta$ | $\tan\theta$ |
|---|---|---|---|
| $30^\circ = \frac{\pi}{6}$ | $\frac12$ | $\frac{\sqrt3}{2}$ | $\frac{1}{\sqrt3} = \frac{\sqrt3}{3}$ |
| $45^\circ = \frac{\pi}{4}$ | $\frac{\sqrt2}{2}$ | $\frac{\sqrt2}{2}$ | $1$ |
| $60^\circ = \frac{\pi}{3}$ | $\frac{\sqrt3}{2}$ | $\frac12$ | $\sqrt3$ |

A pattern helps with recall: the sines of $30^\circ, 45^\circ, 60^\circ$ are
$\tfrac{\sqrt1}{2}, \tfrac{\sqrt2}{2}, \tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}$, and the cosines are the same list
backward. The reciprocals follow: $\csc 30^\circ = 2$, $\sec 30^\circ = \tfrac{2}{\sqrt3} = \tfrac{2\sqrt3}{3}$,
$\cot 60^\circ = \tfrac{\sqrt3}{3}$, and so on.

### Example 1

A 30°–60°–90° triangle has hypotenuse 10. Find both legs.

The short leg is half the hypotenuse: $5$. The long leg is $\sqrt3$ times the short leg:
$5\sqrt3 \approx 8.66$. Check: $5^2 + (5\sqrt3)^2 = 25 + 75 = 100 = 10^2$. ✓

### Example 2

The hypotenuse of a 45°–45°–90° triangle is 8. Find each leg.

The hypotenuse is $\sqrt2$ times a leg, so a leg is $\dfrac{8}{\sqrt2} = \dfrac{8\sqrt2}{2} = 4\sqrt2 \approx 5.66$.
Going the other way, a leg of 7 gives a hypotenuse of $7\sqrt2$.

### Example 3

Find the exact value of $2\sin 30^\circ + \sqrt3\tan 60^\circ - \cos^2 45^\circ$.

Substitute exact values: $2\cdot\tfrac12 + \sqrt3\cdot\sqrt3 - \left(\tfrac{\sqrt2}{2}\right)^2 = 1 + 3 - \tfrac{2}{4} = \tfrac72$.

The notation $\cos^2 45^\circ$ means $(\cos 45^\circ)^2$, not $\cos(45^2)$.

## Cofunctions

In a right triangle the two acute angles add to $90^\circ$, so they are complementary. The
side opposite one is adjacent to the other. That swaps sine with cosine, tangent with
cotangent, and secant with cosecant:

$$\sin\theta = \cos(90^\circ - \theta), \quad \tan\theta = \cot(90^\circ - \theta), \quad \sec\theta = \csc(90^\circ - \theta),$$

and the same with the roles reversed. These are the **[[cofunction identities]]**; in radians,
replace $90^\circ$ with $\tfrac{\pi}{2}$. The name tells the story: **[[cosine]]** is the
*complement's sine*. Sine and cosine (and each pair of a function and its "co-" partner)
are called **[[cofunctions]]**.

### Example 4

Find an acute angle $\theta$ with $\cos\theta = \sin 25^\circ$, and rewrite $\tan 72^\circ$
using a cofunction.

$\sin 25^\circ = \cos(90^\circ - 25^\circ) = \cos 65^\circ$, so $\theta = 65^\circ$.
$\tan 72^\circ = \cot 18^\circ$.

### Example 5: an equilateral triangle from its height

An equilateral triangle has an altitude of 6. Find its side length and area exactly.

The altitude splits it into two 30°–60°–90° triangles in which the altitude is the long leg.
So the short leg is $\tfrac{6}{\sqrt3} = 2\sqrt3$ and the hypotenuse, which is a full side, is $4\sqrt3$.
Area $= \tfrac12 \cdot \text{base} \cdot \text{height} = \tfrac12 \cdot 4\sqrt3 \cdot 6 = 12\sqrt3 \approx 20.78$.

## When to use exact values

Exact values matter whenever later steps would magnify rounding errors, or when a pattern
would be hidden by decimals. $\sin 60^\circ \approx 0.866$ is fine for measuring a roof, but writing
$\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}$ makes it obvious that $\sin^2 60^\circ = \tfrac34$ exactly, which the decimal $0.749956$ only suggests.

## Common mistakes

- **Mixing up which leg goes with which angle.** The short leg is always opposite the
  smallest angle ($30^\circ$). If $\sin 30^\circ$ comes out bigger than $\sin 60^\circ$,
  something is swapped.
- **Doubling instead of halving.** In a 30°–60°–90° triangle the hypotenuse is *twice*
  the short leg, so the short leg is *half* the hypotenuse.
- **Thinking $\tan 30^\circ = \sqrt3$.** $\tan 30^\circ = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt3}$; $\tan 60^\circ = \sqrt3$.
  Small angles have small tangents.
- **Reading $\sin^2\theta$ as $\sin(\theta^2)$.**

## Key points

- 45°–45°–90°: sides $1 : 1 : \sqrt2$. 30°–60°–90°: sides $1 : \sqrt3 : 2$.
- $\sin 30^\circ = \tfrac12$, $\sin 45^\circ = \tfrac{\sqrt2}{2}$, $\sin 60^\circ = \tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}$;
  cosines are the same list reversed.
- $\tan 30^\circ = \tfrac{\sqrt3}{3}$, $\tan 45^\circ = 1$, $\tan 60^\circ = \sqrt3$.
- Cofunction identities: a function of $\theta$ equals its cofunction of $90^\circ - \theta$.

lessons.title: Solving right triangles
lessons.body:
## What "solving" means

A triangle has six parts: three sides and three angles. To **[[solve a triangle]]** is to
find all six from the ones you are given. For a right triangle, one angle is already
known ($90^\circ$), so you need just two more facts, and at least one of them must be a
side. With the trig ratios from the last two lessons, every case reduces to choosing the
right ratio and doing one step of algebra.

## Standard labels

We name the vertices $A$, $B$, $C$ with the right angle at $C$, and write $a$, $b$, $c$ for
the sides *opposite* those vertices. So $c$ is the hypotenuse, $a$ is opposite angle $A$,
and $b$ is opposite angle $B$ (and adjacent to $A$).

```shape
{"polygons": [{"points": [[0, 0], [7, 0], [7, 4]]}], "rightAngles": [[[7, 0], [0, 0], [7, 4]]], "labels": [{"at": [-0.3, -0.3], "text": "A"}, {"at": [7.3, 4.2], "text": "B"}, {"at": [7.3, -0.3], "text": "C"}, {"at": [3.5, -0.45], "text": "b"}, {"at": [7.4, 2], "text": "a"}, {"at": [3.2, 2.4], "text": "c"}]}
```

Two facts hold in every right triangle and serve as checks:

- the acute angles are complementary: $A + B = 90^\circ$;
- the sides satisfy $a^2 + b^2 = c^2$, and $c$ is the longest side. The longest leg is
  across from the larger acute angle.

## Finding a side

If you know an acute angle and one side, pick the ratio that involves the known side and
the side you want, then solve.

### Example 1

Solve the right triangle with $A = 34.5^\circ$ and $c = 18.2$.

**Angle $B$:** $B = 90^\circ - 34.5^\circ = 55.5^\circ$.

**Side $a$ (opposite $A$):** the ratio linking opposite and hypotenuse is sine.
$\sin 34.5^\circ = \dfrac{a}{18.2}$, so $a = 18.2\sin 34.5^\circ \approx 10.3$.

**Side $b$ (adjacent to $A$):** cosine links adjacent and hypotenuse.
$\cos 34.5^\circ = \dfrac{b}{18.2}$, so $b = 18.2\cos 34.5^\circ \approx 15.0$.

**Check:** $10.31^2 + 15.00^2 \approx 106.3 + 225.0 = 331.3$ and $18.2^2 = 331.24$. ✓
The longer leg ($b$) is across from the larger angle ($B$). ✓

When the unknown is in the denominator, it ends up dividing. If $A = 40^\circ$ and $a = 9$,
then $\tan 40^\circ = \tfrac{9}{b}$ gives $b = \dfrac{9}{\tan 40^\circ} \approx 10.73$, not
$9\tan 40^\circ$. Writing the equation before solving prevents that mix-up.

## Finding an angle

If you know two sides, compute the ratio that uses them and then ask "which angle has
this ratio?" The calculator answers that with the **[[inverse trig]]** keys
$\sin^{-1}$, $\cos^{-1}$, $\tan^{-1}$. For an acute angle in a right triangle:

$$\sin A = k \;\Rightarrow\; A = \sin^{-1} k, \qquad \tan A = k \;\Rightarrow\; A = \tan^{-1} k.$$

(The inverse functions are studied properly in Module 5. For now, read $\sin^{-1} k$ as
"the acute angle whose sine is $k$".)

### Example 2

Solve the right triangle with legs $a = 7$ and $b = 11$.

**Hypotenuse:** $c = \sqrt{7^2 + 11^2} = \sqrt{170} \approx 13.04$.

**Angle $A$:** both legs are known, so use tangent. $\tan A = \tfrac{7}{11}$, and
$A = \tan^{-1}\!\left(\tfrac{7}{11}\right) \approx 32.47^\circ$.

**Angle $B$:** $B = 90^\circ - 32.47^\circ = 57.53^\circ$.

Using the original numbers rather than the rounded hypotenuse keeps rounding errors from
piling up. If you did use $c$, $\sin A = 7/13.04$ gives the same angle to two decimals.

## Choosing the ratio

| Known | Want | Use |
|---|---|---|
| angle, hypotenuse | opposite leg | $\sin$: $\text{opp} = \text{hyp}\sin\theta$ |
| angle, hypotenuse | adjacent leg | $\cos$: $\text{adj} = \text{hyp}\cos\theta$ |
| angle, adjacent leg | opposite leg | $\tan$: $\text{opp} = \text{adj}\tan\theta$ |
| angle, a leg | hypotenuse | $\sin$ or $\cos$, then divide |
| two legs | angle | $\tan^{-1}(\text{opp}/\text{adj})$ |
| leg and hypotenuse | angle | $\sin^{-1}$ or $\cos^{-1}$ |

### Example 3

A 20-ft ladder is safe only if it makes an angle of at most $75^\circ$ with the ground.
How high up a wall can it safely reach, and how far from the wall is its foot then?

The ladder is the hypotenuse; the height is opposite the $75^\circ$ angle, the distance
from the wall is adjacent.

Height: $20\sin 75^\circ \approx 19.32$ ft. Distance: $20\cos 75^\circ \approx 5.18$ ft.

```shape
{"polygons": [{"points": [[0, 0], [5.18, 0], [5.18, 19.32]]}], "rightAngles": [[[5.18, 0], [0, 0], [5.18, 19.32]]], "labels": [{"at": [1.0, 1.0], "text": "75°"}, {"at": [2.6, -1.1], "text": "≈ 5.18 ft"}, {"at": [7.6, 9.66], "text": "≈ 19.32 ft"}, {"at": [1.2, 10.5], "text": "20 ft"}], "caption": "The ladder at its steepest safe angle"}
```

## Rounding

Round only the final answers, and keep full calculator precision for intermediate values.
A common convention matches accuracy to the data: sides given to three significant
figures give answers to three significant figures, and angles given to the nearest tenth
of a degree give angles to the nearest tenth.

### Example 4: given the other angle

Solve the right triangle with $B = 62.4^\circ$ and $b = 15.3$.

$A = 90^\circ - 62.4^\circ = 27.6^\circ$. Side $b$ is opposite $B$, so relative to $B$:
$\tan B = \tfrac{b}{a}$ gives $a = \tfrac{15.3}{\tan 62.4^\circ} \approx 8.00$, and $\sin B = \tfrac{b}{c}$ gives
$c = \tfrac{15.3}{\sin 62.4^\circ} \approx 17.26$.

Check: $8.00^2 + 15.3^2 \approx 298.1$ and $17.26^2 \approx 297.9$, equal up to rounding. ✓

## Common mistakes

- **Multiplying when you should divide.** If the unknown is in the denominator
  ($\tan 40^\circ = 9/b$), it ends up as $9/\tan 40^\circ$.
- **Calculator in radian mode.** $\sin 34.5$ in radian mode is about $0.057$, not $0.566$.
- **Forgetting the third angle.** Once one acute angle is known, the other is $90^\circ$ minus it.
- **Using rounded values in later steps.** Carry full precision, round at the end.

## Key points

- Label with $C = 90^\circ$ and sides $a, b, c$ opposite $A, B, C$.
- Angle + side: choose the ratio connecting the known and unknown sides.
- Two sides: use the Pythagorean theorem for the third side and an inverse trig key for
  an angle.
- Check with $A + B = 90^\circ$, $a^2 + b^2 = c^2$, and "longest side opposite largest angle".

lessons.title: Elevation, depression and bearings
lessons.body:
## Measuring what you can't reach

Trigonometry was invented for exactly this: finding the height of a tower, the width of a
river, or the distance to a ship without going there. The method is always the same:
spot a right triangle in the situation, decide which parts you know, and solve it as in
the last lesson. What's new here is the vocabulary used to describe the angles.

## Angles of elevation and depression

Imagine looking at an object. The straight path from your eye to it is the
**[[line of sight]]**.

- If the object is above you, the angle between the horizontal and your line of sight is
  the **[[angle of elevation]]**.
- If the object is below you, the angle between the horizontal and your line of sight is
  the **[[angle of depression]]**.

Both are measured *from the horizontal*, never from the vertical.

```plot
{"x": [-1, 11], "y": [-1, 7], "equal": true, "segments": [{"from": [0, 0], "to": [10, 0], "dashed": true}, {"from": [0, 0], "to": [10, 6]}, {"from": [10, 6], "to": [0, 6], "dashed": true}, {"from": [10, 0], "to": [10, 6]}], "labels": [{"at": [3.2, 0.9], "text": "elevation"}, {"at": [7.6, 5.5], "text": "depression"}, {"at": [5, -0.5], "text": "horizontal"}, {"at": [5, 6.4], "text": "horizontal"}], "points": [{"at": [0, 0], "label": "observer"}, {"at": [10, 6], "label": "top"}], "caption": "Horizontal lines are parallel, so the angle of elevation from below equals the angle of depression from above"}
```

The two horizontal lines are parallel and the line of sight cuts across both, so the
angle of depression from the top equals the angle of elevation from the bottom (they are
alternate interior angles). That lets you move the angle into the right triangle where
you need it.

### Example 1

From a point 50 m from the base of a tree, on level ground, the angle of elevation to the
top is $38^\circ$. The observer's eyes are 1.6 m above the ground. How tall is the tree?

The right triangle has its right angle at eye height on the trunk. The horizontal leg is
50 m (adjacent to $38^\circ$); the vertical leg $h$ is the part of the tree above eye level
(opposite). Tangent links them:
$$\tan 38^\circ = \frac{h}{50} \quad\Rightarrow\quad h = 50\tan 38^\circ \approx 39.06 \text{ m}.$$
Add the eye height: the tree is about $39.06 + 1.6 \approx 40.7$ m tall.

### Example 2

A lighthouse keeper 120 ft above the water sees a boat at an angle of depression of
$9^\circ$. How far is the boat from the base of the lighthouse?

Move the $9^\circ$ to the boat's end as an angle of elevation. Then the 120 ft height is
opposite it and the unknown distance $d$ is adjacent:
$$\tan 9^\circ = \frac{120}{d} \quad\Rightarrow\quad d = \frac{120}{\tan 9^\circ} \approx 757.7 \text{ ft}.$$
The unknown is in the denominator, so it ends up dividing.

### Example 3: two observations

From a point on level ground, the angle of elevation to a mountain peak is $28^\circ$.
After walking 1000 m straight toward the mountain, the angle is $35^\circ$. How high is
the peak above the ground?

Let $h$ be the height and $x$ the remaining horizontal distance from the second point.
There are two right triangles sharing the side $h$:
$$h = x\tan 35^\circ \quad\text{and}\quad h = (x + 1000)\tan 28^\circ.$$
Set them equal and solve for $x$:
$$x\tan 35^\circ = x\tan 28^\circ + 1000\tan 28^\circ \;\Rightarrow\; x = \frac{1000\tan 28^\circ}{\tan 35^\circ - \tan 28^\circ} \approx 3155.6 \text{ m}.$$
Then $h = x\tan 35^\circ \approx 2209.6$ m. Neither triangle alone has enough
information; the shared height ties them together.

```plot
{"x": [-500, 4600], "y": [-300, 2700], "segments": [{"from": [0, 0], "to": [4155.6, 0]}, {"from": [4155.6, 0], "to": [4155.6, 2209.6]}, {"from": [0, 0], "to": [4155.6, 2209.6]}, {"from": [1000, 0], "to": [4155.6, 2209.6]}], "labels": [{"at": [550, 120], "text": "28°"}, {"at": [1500, 120], "text": "35°"}, {"at": [500, -200], "text": "1000 m"}, {"at": [4400, 1100], "text": "h"}], "caption": "Two angles of elevation to the same peak"}
```

## Bearings

Navigators describe directions with **[[bearings]]**. Two notations are common.

- **Three-digit (true) bearing:** the angle measured *clockwise from north*, written with
  three digits. North is $000^\circ$, east $090^\circ$, south $180^\circ$, west $270^\circ$.
- **Quadrant (compass) bearing:** start from north or south, then turn the stated acute
  angle toward east or west. N $35^\circ$ E means "face north, turn $35^\circ$ toward east";
  S $20^\circ$ W means "face south, turn $20^\circ$ toward west".

So N $35^\circ$ E is $035^\circ$, S $20^\circ$ E is $160^\circ$, S $20^\circ$ W is $200^\circ$,
and N $70^\circ$ W is $290^\circ$. Note that bearings are measured from north and turn
clockwise, unlike angles in standard position, which start from east and turn
counterclockwise.

### Example 4

A plane flies 200 mi on a bearing of $040^\circ$, then turns and flies 150 mi on a bearing
of $130^\circ$. How far is it from its starting point, and on what bearing?

The two headings differ by $130^\circ - 40^\circ = 90^\circ$, so the path makes a right
angle at the turn. The legs are 200 and 150:

Distance: $\sqrt{200^2 + 150^2} = 250$ mi.

The angle at the start between the first leg and the line back to the plane is
$\tan^{-1}\!\left(\tfrac{150}{200}\right) \approx 36.87^\circ$, turned clockwise from the first
heading. The bearing is $40^\circ + 36.87^\circ \approx 076.9^\circ$.

### Example 5

A ship sails 40 mi on a course of N $52^\circ$ E. How far north and how far east of its
starting point is it?

The $52^\circ$ is measured from north, so north is the adjacent side:
north $= 40\cos 52^\circ \approx 24.6$ mi and east $= 40\sin 52^\circ \approx 31.5$ mi.
Because the reference direction is north, not east, the roles of sine and cosine are the
reverse of what you might expect.

## Common mistakes

- **Measuring elevation or depression from the vertical.** Both start at the horizontal.
- **Putting the angle of depression at the wrong vertex.** Transfer it to the lower
  object as an equal angle of elevation.
- **Forgetting eye height or platform height** when the question asks for total height.
- **Treating bearings like standard-position angles.** Bearings start at north and go
  clockwise.

## Key points

- Angle of elevation: up from horizontal. Angle of depression: down from horizontal. They
  are equal for the same line of sight.
- Draw the right triangle, label known parts, and solve with the matching ratio.
- With two observation points, write an equation for the shared side in each triangle
  and solve the system.
- Bearing $\theta$ (clockwise from north): north component $= d\cos\theta$, east component
  $= d\sin\theta$.

lessons.title: Trig functions of any angle
lessons.body:
## Beyond the right triangle

A right triangle can only hold acute angles, yet Module 1 described angles of $150^\circ$,
$-45^\circ$ and $1000^\circ$. To give those angles a sine and a cosine, we need a definition
that does not depend on a triangle. The idea is to put the angle in standard position and
use the coordinates of a point on its terminal side. For acute angles the new definition
gives exactly the old values, so nothing learned so far is lost.

## The definition

Put $\theta$ in standard position and pick any point $(x, y)$, other than the origin, on
its terminal side. Let $r = \sqrt{x^2 + y^2}$ be that point's distance from the origin
(always positive). Then

$$\sin\theta = \frac{y}{r}, \quad \cos\theta = \frac{x}{r}, \quad \tan\theta = \frac{y}{x}\ (x \ne 0),$$
$$\csc\theta = \frac{r}{y}\ (y \ne 0), \quad \sec\theta = \frac{r}{x}\ (x \ne 0), \quad \cot\theta = \frac{x}{y}\ (y \ne 0).$$

**Why this extends the old definition:** for an acute angle the point $(x, y)$ is in
quadrant I, and dropping a perpendicular to the $x$-axis makes a right triangle with
adjacent side $x$, opposite side $y$ and hypotenuse $r$. So $y/r$ is opposite over
hypotenuse, as before.

**Why the choice of point doesn't matter:** any other point on the same terminal side is
$(kx, ky)$ with $k > 0$, at distance $kr$, and the $k$'s cancel in every ratio.

```plot
{"x": [-5, 3], "y": [-1.5, 5.5], "equal": true, "segments": [{"from": [0, 0], "to": [-3, 4], "label": "r = 5"}, {"from": [-3, 0], "to": [-3, 4], "dashed": true}], "points": [{"at": [-3, 4], "label": "(−3, 4)"}], "curves": [{"x": "0.6cos(t)", "y": "0.6sin(t)", "t": [0, 2.2143]}], "labels": [{"at": [0.55, 0.6], "text": "θ"}], "caption": "θ in quadrant II with the point (−3, 4) on its terminal side"}
```

### Example 1

The point $(-3, 4)$ is on the terminal side of $\theta$. Find all six trig functions.

**Step 1:** $r = \sqrt{(-3)^2 + 4^2} = \sqrt{25} = 5$.

**Step 2:** substitute $x = -3$, $y = 4$, $r = 5$:
$$\sin\theta = \tfrac45,\ \cos\theta = -\tfrac35,\ \tan\theta = -\tfrac43,\ \csc\theta = \tfrac54,\ \sec\theta = -\tfrac53,\ \cot\theta = -\tfrac34.$$

The signs come automatically from the signs of $x$ and $y$. In quadrant II, $x < 0$ and
$y > 0$, so sine is positive and cosine and tangent are negative.

## Signs in each quadrant

Since $r > 0$, the sign of each function depends only on the signs of $x$ and $y$:

- $\sin\theta = y/r$ has the sign of $y$: positive in quadrants I and II.
- $\cos\theta = x/r$ has the sign of $x$: positive in quadrants I and IV.
- $\tan\theta = y/x$ is positive when $x$ and $y$ agree: quadrants I and III.

Each reciprocal has the same sign as its partner. The mnemonic
**[[All Students Take Calculus]]** (**[[ASTC]]**), read counterclockwise from quadrant I, lists
which functions are positive: **A**ll in I, **S**ine in II, **T**angent in III, **C**osine
in IV.

```plot
{"x": [-2, 2], "y": [-2, 2], "equal": true, "labels": [{"at": [1, 1], "text": "I: All +"}, {"at": [-1, 1], "text": "II: sin, csc +"}, {"at": [-1, -1], "text": "III: tan, cot +"}, {"at": [1, -1], "text": "IV: cos, sec +"}], "caption": "ASTC: which functions are positive in each quadrant"}
```

### Example 2

$\tan\theta = -\tfrac{5}{12}$ and $\cos\theta > 0$. Find $\sin\theta$ and $\sec\theta$.

**Step 1: the quadrant.** Tangent is negative in II and IV; cosine is positive in I and IV.
Both hold only in **quadrant IV**, where $x > 0$, $y < 0$.

**Step 2: a point.** $\tan\theta = \tfrac{y}{x} = \tfrac{-5}{12}$, so take $x = 12$, $y = -5$.
(Not $x = -12$, $y = 5$: that's quadrant II.) Then $r = \sqrt{144 + 25} = 13$.

**Step 3:** $\sin\theta = -\tfrac{5}{13}$ and $\sec\theta = \tfrac{13}{12}$.

This is the standard technique whenever one function value and a sign condition are
given: find the quadrant first, then choose $x$ and $y$ with the right signs.

## Quadrantal angles

For a quadrantal angle the terminal side lies on an axis, so one coordinate is 0. Use the
convenient point at distance $r = 1$:

| $\theta$ | point | $\sin$ | $\cos$ | $\tan$ | $\csc$ | $\sec$ | $\cot$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $0^\circ$ | $(1, 0)$ | $0$ | $1$ | $0$ | undef. | $1$ | undef. |
| $90^\circ$ | $(0, 1)$ | $1$ | $0$ | undef. | $1$ | undef. | $0$ |
| $180^\circ$ | $(-1, 0)$ | $0$ | $-1$ | $0$ | undef. | $-1$ | undef. |
| $270^\circ$ | $(0, -1)$ | $-1$ | $0$ | undef. | $-1$ | undef. | $0$ |

"Undefined" always means a zero in a denominator: tangent and secant divide by $x$, so they
fail where $x = 0$ (at $90^\circ$ and $270^\circ$); cotangent and cosecant divide by $y$, so
they fail where $y = 0$.

### Example 3

Find $\sin 270^\circ$, $\cos 540^\circ$ and $\tan 450^\circ$.

$270^\circ$ ends at $(0, -1)$, so $\sin 270^\circ = -1$.
$540^\circ - 360^\circ = 180^\circ$ ends at $(-1, 0)$, so $\cos 540^\circ = -1$.
$450^\circ - 360^\circ = 90^\circ$ ends at $(0, 1)$, so $\tan 450^\circ = \tfrac10$ is undefined.

Coterminal angles have the same terminal side, hence the same point and the same function
values. That's why reducing to $[0^\circ, 360^\circ)$ first is always allowed.

### Example 4

The terminal side of $\theta$ passes through $(-1, -2)$. Find $\sin\theta$ and $\cos\theta$
exactly.

$r = \sqrt{1 + 4} = \sqrt5$. So $\sin\theta = \tfrac{-2}{\sqrt5} = -\tfrac{2\sqrt5}{5}$ and
$\cos\theta = \tfrac{-1}{\sqrt5} = -\tfrac{\sqrt5}{5}$. Both negative, as expected in quadrant III.

## Common mistakes

- **Giving $r$ a sign.** $r$ is a distance, always positive. All the signs come from $x$ and $y$.
- **Choosing the point with the wrong signs** when working from a ratio like
  $\tan\theta = -\tfrac{5}{12}$. Decide the quadrant first.
- **Saying $\tan 90^\circ = 0$ or $\infty$.** It is undefined (division by zero).
- **Dropping the sign of a coordinate** when computing $r$: $(-3)^2 = 9$, not $-9$.

## Key points

- With $(x, y)$ on the terminal side and $r = \sqrt{x^2 + y^2}$: $\sin\theta = y/r$,
  $\cos\theta = x/r$, $\tan\theta = y/x$, and the reciprocals.
- ASTC: All, Sine, Tangent, Cosine are positive in quadrants I, II, III, IV.
- Quadrantal angles: use $(\pm1, 0)$ or $(0, \pm1)$; a zero denominator means undefined.
- Coterminal angles have identical trig values.

lessons.title: Reference angles
lessons.body:
## Reducing every angle to an acute one

The last lesson defined the trig functions for every angle, but evaluating, say,
$\cos 210^\circ$ exactly still needs a shortcut. The shortcut is the reference angle: every
angle's trig values are the same, up to sign, as those of an acute angle. Combined with
the special triangles and the ASTC sign rule, it gives exact values for a huge family of
angles.

## Definition

The **[[reference angle]]** of $\theta$ is the acute angle $\theta'$ between the terminal side
of $\theta$ and the $x$-axis (never the $y$-axis). It is always between $0^\circ$ and
$90^\circ$ (or between $0$ and $\tfrac{\pi}{2}$).

First reduce $\theta$ to the coterminal angle in $[0^\circ, 360^\circ)$, then:

| Quadrant of $\theta$ | Reference angle $\theta'$ (degrees) | (radians) |
|---|---|---|
| I | $\theta$ | $\theta$ |
| II | $180^\circ - \theta$ | $\pi - \theta$ |
| III | $\theta - 180^\circ$ | $\theta - \pi$ |
| IV | $360^\circ - \theta$ | $2\pi - \theta$ |

In every case you measure the shortest way back to the $x$-axis.

```plot
{"x": [-1.5, 1.5], "y": [-1.5, 1.5], "equal": true, "segments": [{"from": [0, 0], "to": [1.3, 0]}, {"from": [0, 0], "to": [-1.0392, -0.6], "arrow": true}], "curves": [{"x": "0.35cos(t)", "y": "0.35sin(t)", "t": [0, 3.6652]}, {"x": "0.75cos(t)", "y": "0.75sin(t)", "t": [3.1416, 3.6652], "color": "#d9480f"}], "labels": [{"at": [0.35, 0.45], "text": "210°"}, {"at": [-0.95, -0.22], "text": "30°"}], "caption": "The reference angle of 210° is 210° − 180° = 30°"}
```

## Why it works

Let $P = (x, y)$ be the point at distance 1 on the terminal side of $\theta$, and $Q$ the
point at distance 1 on the terminal side of $\theta'$ (in quadrant I). The terminal side of
$\theta$ is the reflection of the terminal side of $\theta'$ across the $x$-axis, the
$y$-axis, or both. Reflections only flip signs of coordinates, so $P$ and $Q$ have the same
coordinates *up to sign*. Every trig function is built from those coordinates, so

$$\text{trig}(\theta) = \pm\,\text{trig}(\theta'),$$

where the sign is decided by the quadrant of $\theta$ (ASTC).

## The three-step method

1. Find the reference angle $\theta'$.
2. Evaluate the function at $\theta'$ (a special triangle, or a calculator).
3. Attach the sign the function has in $\theta$'s quadrant.

### Example 1

Find the reference angle of (a) $150^\circ$, (b) $225^\circ$, (c) $-130^\circ$,
(d) $\tfrac{5\pi}{3}$, (e) 4 radians.

**(a)** Quadrant II: $180^\circ - 150^\circ = 30^\circ$.

**(b)** Quadrant III: $225^\circ - 180^\circ = 45^\circ$.

**(c)** First $-130^\circ + 360^\circ = 230^\circ$, quadrant III: $230^\circ - 180^\circ = 50^\circ$.

**(d)** $\tfrac{5\pi}{3}$ is between $\tfrac{3\pi}{2}$ and $2\pi$, quadrant IV:
$2\pi - \tfrac{5\pi}{3} = \tfrac{\pi}{3}$.

**(e)** $\pi \approx 3.14 < 4 < 4.71 \approx \tfrac{3\pi}{2}$, quadrant III:
$4 - \pi \approx 0.858$ radians.

### Example 2

Find exact values of $\cos 210^\circ$, $\tan(-300^\circ)$ and $\sec\tfrac{5\pi}{4}$.

**$\cos 210^\circ$.** Reference angle $30^\circ$; $\cos 30^\circ = \tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}$.
Quadrant III, where cosine is negative: $\cos 210^\circ = -\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}$.

**$\tan(-300^\circ)$.** Coterminal with $60^\circ$, which is in quadrant I and is its own
reference angle. So $\tan(-300^\circ) = \tan 60^\circ = \sqrt3$. (Positive, even though the
original angle was negative: what matters is where the terminal side lands.)

**$\sec\tfrac{5\pi}{4}$.** Reference angle $\tfrac{\pi}{4}$; $\sec\tfrac{\pi}{4} = \sqrt2$.
Quadrant III, where secant (like cosine) is negative: $\sec\tfrac{5\pi}{4} = -\sqrt2$.

### Example 3

Without a calculator's help for the sign, express $\sin 155^\circ$ and $\cos 155^\circ$ in
terms of an acute angle and approximate them.

Reference angle $25^\circ$, quadrant II. Sine is positive there and cosine negative:
$$\sin 155^\circ = \sin 25^\circ \approx 0.4226, \qquad \cos 155^\circ = -\cos 25^\circ \approx -0.9063.$$

### Example 4: working backward

Find all $\theta$ in $[0^\circ, 360^\circ)$ with $\sin\theta = -\tfrac12$.

$\sin\theta' = \tfrac12$ gives the reference angle $30^\circ$. Sine is negative in
quadrants III and IV, so
$$\theta = 180^\circ + 30^\circ = 210^\circ \quad\text{or}\quad \theta = 360^\circ - 30^\circ = 330^\circ.$$
This reverse use of reference angles is the heart of solving trig equations (Module 5).

### Example 5: radians and reciprocal functions

Find $\csc\left(-\tfrac{5\pi}{6}\right)$ and $\cot\tfrac{11\pi}{4}$ exactly.

**$\csc\left(-\tfrac{5\pi}{6}\right)$.** Add $2\pi$: the angle is coterminal with $\tfrac{7\pi}{6}$, in quadrant III. Reference
angle $\tfrac{\pi}{6}$, and $\sin\tfrac{\pi}{6} = \tfrac12$. Sine (and so cosecant) is negative in quadrant III:
$\sin\left(-\tfrac{5\pi}{6}\right) = -\tfrac12$ and $\csc\left(-\tfrac{5\pi}{6}\right) = -2$.

**$\cot\tfrac{11\pi}{4}$.** Subtract $2\pi = \tfrac{8\pi}{4}$: coterminal with $\tfrac{3\pi}{4}$, in quadrant II. Reference angle $\tfrac{\pi}{4}$
with $\cot\tfrac{\pi}{4} = 1$; cotangent is negative in quadrant II, so $\cot\tfrac{11\pi}{4} = -1$.

## Why bother when calculators exist?

A calculator returns $\cos 210^\circ \approx -0.8660$ instantly, but it can't tell you that this is exactly
$-\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}$, and it can't run the problem backward to list *every* angle with that cosine.
Reference angles do both. They also catch calculator errors: if a calculator says
$\sin 155^\circ$ is negative, you know at once the mode is wrong.

## The reference angle as a picture

A good habit is to sketch the angle before computing. Draw the terminal side roughly where
it belongs, then shade the thin wedge between it and the nearest part of the $x$-axis. That
wedge *is* the reference angle, and the quadrant the terminal side sits in gives the sign.
The whole method takes a few seconds once the sketch is automatic.

## Common mistakes

- **Measuring to the $y$-axis.** The reference angle of $120^\circ$ is $60^\circ$ (to the
  negative $x$-axis), not $30^\circ$.
- **Forgetting to reduce first.** For $-130^\circ$ or $480^\circ$, find the coterminal angle in
  $[0^\circ, 360^\circ)$ before applying the table.
- **Losing the sign.** The reference angle gives the size of the value; the quadrant gives
  the sign. $\cos 210^\circ$ is $-\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}$, not $\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}$.
- **Mixing units.** In radians, subtract from $\pi$ or $2\pi$, not from $180$ or $360$.

## Key points

- The reference angle is the acute angle to the nearest part of the $x$-axis.
- QII: $180^\circ - \theta$; QIII: $\theta - 180^\circ$; QIV: $360^\circ - \theta$
  (or $\pi - \theta$, $\theta - \pi$, $2\pi - \theta$).
- $\text{trig}(\theta) = \pm\,\text{trig}(\theta')$ with the sign from ASTC.
- Running the method backward finds every angle with a given trig value.

lessons.title: The unit circle
lessons.body:
## One circle that holds every value

The definition $\sin\theta = y/r$ works with any point on the terminal side. Choosing the
point at distance $r = 1$ removes the denominator completely: the coordinates of that
point *are* the cosine and sine. The set of all such points is the unit circle, and it is
the single most useful picture in trigonometry. It also turns sine and cosine into
functions of a real number, which is what graphs (next module), calculus and physics need.

## The unit circle and its points

The **[[unit circle]]** is the circle of radius 1 centered at the origin:
$$x^2 + y^2 = 1.$$
If the terminal side of $\theta$ meets the unit circle at $(x, y)$, then $r = 1$ and

$$\cos\theta = x, \qquad \sin\theta = y, \qquad \tan\theta = \frac{y}{x}.$$

So **cosine is the $x$-coordinate and sine is the $y$-coordinate** of the point on the
unit circle. Since the point is on the circle, $x^2 + y^2 = 1$ becomes
$\cos^2\theta + \sin^2\theta = 1$, the most important identity in the subject (Module 6
builds on it).

Both coordinates of a point on the unit circle lie between $-1$ and $1$, which shows at a
glance that $-1 \le \sin\theta \le 1$ and $-1 \le \cos\theta \le 1$.

## Angles as real numbers

On the unit circle, a central angle of $t$ radians subtends an arc of length
$s = r t = t$. So the radian measure of the angle equals the arc length walked along the
circle from $(1, 0)$. This lets us define sine and cosine of any real number $t$: walk a
distance $t$ around the unit circle (counterclockwise if $t > 0$, clockwise if $t < 0$),
and read off the point's coordinates. Defined this way, sine and cosine are sometimes
called **[[circular functions]]**; the point you land on is the **[[terminal point]]** of $t$.

## Filling in the circle

The special triangles give the quadrant I points:

- $t = \tfrac{\pi}{6}$ ($30^\circ$): $\left(\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}, \tfrac12\right)$
- $t = \tfrac{\pi}{4}$ ($45^\circ$): $\left(\tfrac{\sqrt2}{2}, \tfrac{\sqrt2}{2}\right)$
- $t = \tfrac{\pi}{3}$ ($60^\circ$): $\left(\tfrac12, \tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\right)$

Every other special point is a reflection of one of these, with signs set by the
quadrant. That is the reference-angle idea from the last lesson, now as a picture.

```plot
{"x": [-1.6, 1.6], "y": [-1.6, 1.6], "equal": true, "circles": [{"center": [0, 0], "r": 1}], "points": [{"at": [0.866, 0.5], "label": "(√3/2, 1/2)"}, {"at": [0.7071, 0.7071]}, {"at": [0.5, 0.866], "label": "(1/2, √3/2)"}, {"at": [-0.866, 0.5], "label": "(−√3/2, 1/2)"}, {"at": [-0.7071, 0.7071]}, {"at": [-0.5, 0.866]}, {"at": [-0.866, -0.5], "label": "(−√3/2, −1/2)"}, {"at": [-0.7071, -0.7071]}, {"at": [-0.5, -0.866]}, {"at": [0.866, -0.5], "label": "(√3/2, −1/2)"}, {"at": [0.7071, -0.7071]}, {"at": [0.5, -0.866]}, {"at": [1, 0]}, {"at": [0, 1]}, {"at": [-1, 0]}, {"at": [0, -1]}], "caption": "Special points on the unit circle; each quadrant mirrors quadrant I"}
```

The full table with all sixteen points is on the reference sheet. Rather than memorizing
48 numbers, notice:

- Points with denominator 6 ($\tfrac{\pi}{6}, \tfrac{5\pi}{6}, \tfrac{7\pi}{6}, \tfrac{11\pi}{6}$)
  are close to the $x$-axis, so $|x| = \tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}$ (big) and $|y| = \tfrac12$ (small).
- Points with denominator 3 are close to the $y$-axis: $|x| = \tfrac12$, $|y| = \tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}$.
- Points with denominator 4 sit on the diagonals: $|x| = |y| = \tfrac{\sqrt2}{2}$.
- The signs come from the quadrant.

### Example 1

Find the terminal point on the unit circle for $t = \tfrac{7\pi}{6}$ and for
$t = \tfrac{3\pi}{4}$.

$\tfrac{7\pi}{6} = \pi + \tfrac{\pi}{6}$ is a sixth of a half turn past $\pi$: quadrant III,
near the negative $x$-axis. So the point is $\left(-\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}, -\tfrac12\right)$.

$\tfrac{3\pi}{4} = \pi - \tfrac{\pi}{4}$: quadrant II, on the diagonal. The point is
$\left(-\tfrac{\sqrt2}{2}, \tfrac{\sqrt2}{2}\right)$.

### Example 2

Evaluate $\sin\tfrac{11\pi}{6}$, $\cos\left(-\tfrac{2\pi}{3}\right)$ and $\tan\tfrac{5\pi}{3}$.

**$\sin\tfrac{11\pi}{6}$:** $\tfrac{11\pi}{6} = 2\pi - \tfrac{\pi}{6}$, quadrant IV, near the
$x$-axis: point $\left(\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}, -\tfrac12\right)$. Sine is the $y$-coordinate: $-\tfrac12$.

**$\cos\left(-\tfrac{2\pi}{3}\right)$:** walking $\tfrac{2\pi}{3}$ clockwise lands in quadrant III
(coterminal with $\tfrac{4\pi}{3}$), near the $y$-axis: point $\left(-\tfrac12, -\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\right)$.
Cosine is the $x$-coordinate: $-\tfrac12$.

**$\tan\tfrac{5\pi}{3}$:** quadrant IV near the $y$-axis: $\left(\tfrac12, -\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\right)$.
$\tan = \tfrac{y}{x} = \tfrac{-\sqrt3/2}{1/2} = -\sqrt3$.

### Example 3

The point $\left(-\tfrac35, y\right)$ is on the unit circle in quadrant III, and is the
terminal point of $t$. Find $\sin t$ and $\tan t$.

From $x^2 + y^2 = 1$: $y^2 = 1 - \tfrac{9}{25} = \tfrac{16}{25}$, so $y = \pm\tfrac45$. In
quadrant III, $y < 0$: $y = -\tfrac45$. Then $\sin t = -\tfrac45$ and
$\tan t = \tfrac{-4/5}{-3/5} = \tfrac43$.

## Reading the other functions off the circle

With $(x, y)$ on the unit circle: $\tan t = \tfrac{y}{x}$, $\cot t = \tfrac{x}{y}$,
$\sec t = \tfrac1x$, $\csc t = \tfrac1y$. Tangent is also the slope of the terminal side,
since the line through the origin and $(x, y)$ has slope $y/x$. That's a quick way to see
why $\tan t$ is undefined at $\tfrac{\pi}{2}$ (a vertical line has no slope) and why
$\tan\tfrac{\pi}{4} = 1$ (the diagonal has slope 1).

### Example 4: reading the circle backward

Find every $t$ in $[0, 2\pi)$ whose terminal point has $y$-coordinate $\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}$.

The horizontal line $y = \tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}$ meets the unit circle twice, at points near the $y$-axis (since
$\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}$ is the big value): $\left(\tfrac12, \tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\right)$ at $t = \tfrac{\pi}{3}$ and $\left(-\tfrac12, \tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\right)$ at $t = \tfrac{2\pi}{3}$.

## Common mistakes

- **Swapping sine and cosine.** Cosine is $x$ (first coordinate), sine is $y$. Alphabetical
  order helps: $c$ before $s$, $x$ before $y$.
- **Swapping the $\tfrac12$ and $\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}$.** At $\tfrac{\pi}{6}$ the point is close to the
  $x$-axis, so its $y$-coordinate (the sine) is the small one, $\tfrac12$.
- **Wrong sign from the quadrant.** Picture where the point is before writing it.
- **Forgetting that $t$ can be any real number.** $\sin(-\tfrac{\pi}{2})$ and $\cos(5\pi)$ make
  perfect sense: walk around the circle.

## Key points

- Unit circle: $x^2 + y^2 = 1$. The point for angle $t$ is $(\cos t, \sin t)$.
- Radian measure on the unit circle equals arc length, so sine and cosine are functions
  of any real number.
- Quadrant I points: $\left(\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}, \tfrac12\right)$, $\left(\tfrac{\sqrt2}{2}, \tfrac{\sqrt2}{2}\right)$,
  $\left(\tfrac12, \tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\right)$; reflect them for the other quadrants.
- $\tan t = y/x$ is the slope of the terminal side.

lessons.title: Domain, range, periodicity and symmetry
lessons.body:
## Reading properties off the unit circle

Now that sine and cosine are functions of any real number, we can ask the usual function
questions: what inputs are allowed, what outputs are possible, and what symmetry the
function has. Every answer can be read from the unit circle, and these properties are
exactly what shape the graphs in the next module. They also give fast ways to evaluate
expressions like $\sin\tfrac{25\pi}{6}$ or $\cos(-t)$.

## Domain and range

Every real number $t$ gives a point $(\cos t, \sin t)$ on the unit circle, so sine and
cosine have **[[domain]]** all real numbers. The coordinates of points on the unit circle
take every value from $-1$ to $1$ and no others, so their **[[range]]** is $[-1, 1]$.

The other four functions are quotients, and are undefined where the denominator is zero:

- $\tan t = \tfrac{\sin t}{\cos t}$ and $\sec t = \tfrac{1}{\cos t}$ fail where $\cos t = 0$, that is
  at $t = \tfrac{\pi}{2} + k\pi$ for integers $k$ (the top and bottom of the circle).
- $\cot t = \tfrac{\cos t}{\sin t}$ and $\csc t = \tfrac{1}{\sin t}$ fail where $\sin t = 0$, at
  $t = k\pi$.

Ranges: tangent and cotangent take every real value. Secant and cosecant are reciprocals
of numbers between $-1$ and $1$, so their absolute value is at least 1: the range is
$(-\infty, -1] \cup [1, \infty)$.

| Function | Domain | Range |
|---|---|---|
| $\sin t$, $\cos t$ | all reals | $[-1, 1]$ |
| $\tan t$, $\sec t$ | $t \ne \tfrac{\pi}{2} + k\pi$ | all reals; $\lvert\sec t\rvert \ge 1$ |
| $\cot t$, $\csc t$ | $t \ne k\pi$ | all reals; $\lvert\csc t\rvert \ge 1$ |

## Periodicity

Walking an extra $2\pi$ around the unit circle returns you to the same point, so
$$\sin(t + 2\pi) = \sin t, \qquad \cos(t + 2\pi) = \cos t.$$

A function $f$ is **[[periodic]]** if there is a positive number $p$ with $f(t + p) = f(t)$
for every $t$ in its domain. The smallest such $p$ is the **[[period]]**. Sine, cosine,
secant and cosecant have period $2\pi$.

Tangent and cotangent repeat twice as fast. Walking half a turn ($\pi$) takes $(x, y)$ to
the opposite point $(-x, -y)$, and
$$\tan(t + \pi) = \frac{-y}{-x} = \frac{y}{x} = \tan t.$$
So tangent and cotangent have period $\pi$.

Periodicity lets you strip whole periods from an angle before evaluating.

### Example 1

Evaluate $\sin\tfrac{25\pi}{6}$, $\cos(-7\pi)$ and $\tan\tfrac{13\pi}{4}$.

**$\sin\tfrac{25\pi}{6}$:** $\tfrac{25\pi}{6} = 4\pi + \tfrac{\pi}{6}$. Remove two full periods:
$\sin\tfrac{\pi}{6} = \tfrac12$.

**$\cos(-7\pi)$:** $-7\pi = -8\pi + \pi$, so $\cos(-7\pi) = \cos\pi = -1$.

**$\tan\tfrac{13\pi}{4}$:** tangent's period is $\pi$, and $\tfrac{13\pi}{4} = 3\pi + \tfrac{\pi}{4}$:
$\tan\tfrac{\pi}{4} = 1$.

## Even and odd

Compare $t$ and $-t$. Walking the same distance in opposite directions from $(1, 0)$ gives
two points that are mirror images across the $x$-axis: $(x, y)$ and $(x, -y)$.

```plot
{"x": [-1.5, 1.5], "y": [-1.5, 1.5], "equal": true, "circles": [{"center": [0, 0], "r": 1}], "segments": [{"from": [0, 0], "to": [0.6, 0.8]}, {"from": [0, 0], "to": [0.6, -0.8]}, {"from": [0.6, 0.8], "to": [0.6, -0.8], "dashed": true}], "points": [{"at": [0.6, 0.8], "label": "(x, y): t"}, {"at": [0.6, -0.8], "label": "(x, −y): −t"}], "caption": "t and −t: same x-coordinate, opposite y-coordinates"}
```

So
$$\cos(-t) = \cos t, \qquad \sin(-t) = -\sin t, \qquad \tan(-t) = -\tan t.$$

A function with $f(-t) = f(t)$ is an **[[even function]]** (its graph is symmetric about the
$y$-axis); one with $f(-t) = -f(t)$ is an **[[odd function]]** (symmetric about the origin).
Cosine is even; sine and tangent are odd. The reciprocals inherit the property: secant is
even, cosecant and cotangent are odd. Only the "cos" pair (cosine and secant) is even.

### Example 2

Given $\sin t = 0.3$ and $\cos t = -0.954$ (rounded), find $\sin(-t)$, $\cos(-t)$,
$\tan(-t)$ and $\cos(t + 2\pi)$.

$\sin(-t) = -\sin t = -0.3$. $\cos(-t) = \cos t = -0.954$.
$\tan(-t) = -\tan t = -\tfrac{0.3}{-0.954} \approx 0.314$. $\cos(t + 2\pi) = \cos t = -0.954$.

### Example 3

Is $f(x) = x\sin x$ even, odd or neither? What about $g(x) = \sin x + \cos x$?

$f(-x) = (-x)\sin(-x) = (-x)(-\sin x) = x\sin x = f(x)$: **[[even]]**.

$g(-x) = \sin(-x) + \cos(-x) = -\sin x + \cos x$. That is neither $g(x)$ nor $-g(x)$ (try
$x = \tfrac{\pi}{4}$: $g = \sqrt2$, $g(-x) = 0$), so $g$ is **neither**.

### Example 4

Simplify $\sin(-t)\csc t + \cos(-t)\sec t$.

$\sin(-t)\csc t = -\sin t\cdot\tfrac{1}{\sin t} = -1$ and $\cos(-t)\sec t = \cos t\cdot\tfrac{1}{\cos t} = 1$.
The sum is $0$ (wherever both terms are defined).

### Example 5: combining the properties

$\tan t = -\tfrac34$ with $t$ in quadrant II. Find $\tan(-t)$, $\tan(t + \pi)$ and $\sec(-t)$.

$\tan(-t) = -\tan t = \tfrac34$ (odd). $\tan(t + \pi) = \tan t = -\tfrac34$ (period $\pi$).
